Extract model estimates and analysis results

Source: R/get-data.R
get_results.Rd

get_results() provides access to the estimates and summaries produced by models and analyses in latents. It supports examination of the estimated latent classes, their membership probabilities, and model-fit statistics, as well as the preparation of results for reporting and further analysis.

The results available depend on the supplied object. Fitted models provide measurement estimates, class proportions, posterior membership probabilities, and other model-specific quantities, such as transition probabilities. Enumeration and comparison objects provide summaries of candidate models, while diagnostic and bootstrap objects provide their corresponding checks and test results.

The what argument selects the requested table. Each table is returned as a standard R data frame, allowing its contents to be inspected, filtered, combined, or exported. Omitting what returns the object's primary table; what = "all" returns a named collection of the tables included by default for that object.

Usage

get_results(x, what = NULL, ...)

Arguments

x

A fitted model of this package, an enumeration grid, a model comparison, a bootstrap comparison, a starting-value set, a classification-diagnostics object, or the summary of any of them.

what

Name of the table to return, or "all" for the collection of tables included by default for the object. NULL (default) returns the primary table: the measurement model for a fit, the candidate grid for an enumeration, the test row for a bootstrap comparison and the entropy table for a diagnostics object. A name the object does not offer raises latents_bad_argument, listing the names it does offer.

...

Arguments for the requested table. Each table accepts only the arguments listed for it under Tables; any other argument raises latents_bad_argument.

Value

A base data.frame for a single what, whose columns are given under Tables, or a named list of such data frames for what = "all".

Details

Some tables calculate additional quantities when requested. For example, measurement tables may obtain standard errors through parameter_inference(). Their availability therefore depends on the fitted model and the requirements of the corresponding calculation.

The table catalogue below specifies the contents and accepted arguments of each table, including results that require an explicit request.

Every object also has print(), which shows a compact overview, summary(), which collects its main tables (taking level and vcov_type where the model has standard errors), and as.data.frame(), which returns its primary table, the same as get_results(x).

Before combining supplied data with model results, the function checks row alignment using columns retained by the fitted object, such as identifiers, occasions, and indicators. Numeric values serialized by utils::write.csv() are also accepted when serialization preserves distinct values. Columns absent from the fitted object cannot establish alignment. Inference and model comparison apply additional checks to verify that supplied data reproduce the estimation data.

Tables

The following tables apply to profile and class models and, where supported, membership-covariate and transition models. Tables for other model families are described in Tables of the other model families.

"profiles"

The Gaussian measurement model, one row per profile and continuous indicator: profile, indicator, mean, variance, standard_deviation, mean_standard_error, variance_standard_error. Zero rows, with the same columns, when every indicator is categorical. Takes scale and data.

"responses"

The categorical measurement model, one row per profile, categorical indicator and category: profile, indicator, category, probability, threshold, probability_standard_error. threshold is qlogis(P(y <= category)) and is NA_real_ for each indicator's final category; a probability on its bound has an NA_real_ standard error. Zero rows, with the same columns, when no indicator is categorical. Takes data.

"covariances"

The within-profile residual covariance matrices, one row per profile and ordered pair of continuous indicators: profile, indicator, indicator_2, covariance. Under the diagonal parameterization the off-diagonal covariances are reported as exact zeros.

"ordinal", "count_means"

Fits with ordinal or count indicators only: the ordinal and count measurement models. Take data.

"counts"

Effective class sizes, one row per class at each level of the fit: level, class, effective_count (the summed posteriors) and effective_proportion. Effective counts use posterior probabilities; modal counts in "classification" use discrete class assignments.

"model"

One row describing the fit: its dimensions, likelihood, parameter counts, aic, bic_groups, bic_individual and its convergence and boundary diagnostics. The columns differ by family (a covariate fit adds its predictor counts); "information_criteria" has the same columns for every family.

"posteriors"

One row per individual and profile: row, group, profile, posterior, modal. Takes format. Excluded observations retain their rows, with posterior and modal set to NA. In wide format their assigned profile and posterior columns are NA.

"assignments"

One row per observation: the columns the fit was built from (or those of data), then profile, group_class where the model has one, uncertainty (one minus the posterior of the assigned profile) and one posterior_profile_* column per profile, plus posterior_noise for a fit with a noise component (whose cases are profile 0). Takes data and truth; with truth it returns a recovery table instead (see Recovery). Row order is preserved. Under the default drop_empty = TRUE, observations with no observed indicators have NA for profile, uncertainty and the posterior columns. Group assignments are missing only when the entire group is excluded; an empty observation can therefore retain a group assignment supported by other observations. Zero-weight units are unclassified under either drop_empty setting.

"classification"

Classification quality, one row per level and class: level, class, n_modal, proportion_modal, estimated_n, estimated_proportion, average_posterior, odds_correct_classification. Takes level. Under sampling weights every column that estimates the population is weighted: estimated_n and estimated_proportion are weighted posterior totals and average_posterior a weighted mean, so the odds of correct classification compare the two on the same population; n_modal and proportion_modal stay counts of the units supplied. The odds are Inf for a class classified perfectly (average posterior one to within rounding) and NA where they are undefined: a class with no modal members, or a single class, whose proportion is one.

"average_posteriors"

For the units modally assigned to each class, their mean posterior for every class: level, assigned_class, class, n_assigned, average_posterior. Rows sum to one within each assigned class. Under sampling weights average_posterior is the weighted mean and n_assigned stays a count. This conditions on the assigned class, whereas "classification_errors" conditions on the true class. Takes level.

"classification_errors"

The probability that a unit in one true class is assigned to another: level, true_class, assigned_class, probability, summing to one within each true_class. Takes level. It is sum_i w_i p_it 1(W_i = s) / sum_i w_i p_it for true class t and assigned class s (Vermunt 2010), with w_i the unit's sampling weight under sampling weights and 1 otherwise, so a weighted fit reports the population's error rates. On a membership-covariate fit this is a marginal summary over the fitted units, not conditional on the covariates. A fit with a noise component raises latents_unsupported_noise, as three_step() does, and "all" and summary() omit the table.

"bch_weights"

The BCH inverse-error weights, one row per unit and class: level, unit, assigned_class, class, weight. Takes level; a weighted regression should use one level, not "both". They invert the "classification_errors" matrix, weighted as it is. On a membership-covariate fit the weights invert the marginal error matrix and are not a conditional three-step correction. Not available for a fit with a noise component, as for "classification_errors".

"entropy"

One row per level: level, n_classes, n_units, entropy_sum, relative_entropy. Under sampling weights entropy_sum is sum_i w_i e_i and relative_entropy 1 - sum_i w_i e_i / (sum_i w_i log K); n_units stays a count.

"replication"

One row: n_starts (starts run to the end), n_best_replicated (those whose log likelihood is within tolerance of the best), share, tolerance, best_start (the selected start's index) and log_likelihood. A best solution reached by one start of several may not be the global maximum: refit with more starts.

"residuals"

Bivariate residuals for every pair of indicators, checking within-profile independence: profile, indicator_1, indicator_2, kind ("gaussian", "categorical", "mixed" or "count"), observed, expected, residual, effective_n, statistic, df, p_value, p_adjusted. Takes data, by and adjust. See Bivariate residuals for what each kind computes.

"information_criteria"

Every information criterion the package computes (see Information criteria). Takes format and definitions.

"sequences"

The assignments in occasion order, one row per classified observation (a row with nothing observed is left out, or kept under drop_empty = FALSE): group, group_class, time, profile. Takes format. Raises latents_no_time for a fit made without time.

"sequence_summary"

One row per group class: group_class, groups, observations, mean_length, median_length, shortest, longest, complete, gaps. Summarises classified groups only; lengths describe their recorded occasions, including occasions with missing indicators. Raises latents_no_time for a fit made without time.

"starts"

One row per EM start: start, log_likelihood, converged, iterations, error and, where the family records it, boundary. Under search = "emEM", one row per start of the pool, with its kind, its stage ("final" when run to convergence, "screened" otherwise) and its screened_log_likelihood.

"data"

The data the model was fitted to, one row per observation in input order: the identifier (except for a single-level fit), the occasion where there is one, the sampling weights of a weighted fit (as rescaled for fitting) and the indicators under their original names. Columns the model did not use, including membership covariates, are not included; three_step() and r3step() therefore take data.

Fits with discrete group classes also offer:

"group_posteriors"

One row per observed group and group class: group, group_size, log_likelihood, group_class, posterior, modal. Takes format. Excluded groups retain their rows, with missing posterior probabilities and modal assignments, as for "posteriors".

Tables specific to one family or object:

"gaussian_diagnostics"

Gaussian profile, membership-covariate, transition and cross-level fits that record these diagnostics. One row per Gaussian component and measurement context: context, profile, gaussian_mass, positive_rows, weight_effective_n, min_variance_ratio, min_standardized_eigenvalue, boundary. gaussian_mass sums posterior times normalized sampling weight over rows with at least one observed Gaussian indicator; positive_rows counts those rows (the same for every component, since a Gaussian density is positive everywhere). weight_effective_n is the concentration measure (sum(a)^2 / sum(a^2)) for those contributions, not an identification guarantee; Gaussian mass is not this effective sample size. min_variance_ratio is the smallest component variance divided by its observed sampling-weighted marginal variance on the fitted scale, including between-component variation. min_standardized_eigenvalue is the smallest eigenvalue of the component covariance after standardizing every indicator by its observed sampling-weighted marginal standard deviation. Missing reference variation gives NA ratios. boundary concerns the absolute variance or eigenvalue floor. These descriptive measures use no automatic spike cutoff and do not alter start selection.

"profile_probabilities", "stages"

A multilpa fit. "profile_probabilities" has one row per group class and profile: group_class, profile, probability, group_class_probability. "stages" has one row per estimation stage: stage, group_classes, fixed, log_likelihood, parameters, parameters_with_measurement, converged. An ordinary fit has one "joint" row and a fit_staged() result has two; fixed is NA_character_ for a stage that estimated every block.

"coefficients"

A covariate fit. One row per estimated membership coefficient: level ("profile" or "group"), outcome, term, parameter (always "logit"), estimate. Standard errors are given by parameter_inference().

"transitions", "initial", "sequence_lengths"

A transition fit. "transitions" has one row per group class and ordered pair of profiles: group_class, from, to, probability, expected_count, stable, estimated, group_class_probability; it takes estimated and stable. "initial" has one row per group class and profile: group_class, profile, probability, prevalence, group_class_probability. "sequence_lengths" has one row per group: group, group_class, occasions, observations, complete.

"candidates", "best", "classification"

An enumeration grid. "candidates" has one row per candidate model: its name (candidate, first), its class counts, covariance model, log likelihood, parameter count, every criterion under both sample-size conventions, both entropies, the average posterior probability (AvePP) summaries of each level (avepp_min, avepp_max, avepp_mean, avepp_below and the same four prefixed group_) and the convergence, boundary, replication, warning and error diagnostics, including min_standardized_eigenvalue and min_gaussian_mass where Gaussian diagnostics are available. These are descriptive summaries, without an automatic cutoff or change to candidate selection. Failed candidates are kept with NA estimates and their error text. It takes cutoff (default 0.8): avepp_below and group_avepp_below count the classes whose AvePP is below it. A class with no modally assigned unit has no AvePP; it is excluded from the minimum, maximum and mean and counted as below the cutoff. A level with one class has NA summaries. "best" has one row per information criterion and sample-size convention: criterion, convention, candidate (the converged candidate with the lowest value), n_profiles, n_group_classes, model and value; what = "criteria" is accepted as a deprecated name for it. "classification" has one row per fitted candidate, level and class: candidate, n_profiles, n_group_classes, model, then the columns of a fit's "classification" table and that level's relative_entropy. Failed candidates and single-class levels contribute no rows.

"deltas", "knees"

Model-selection evidence of an enumeration grid, each taking using (default "bic_groups"). Neither selects a model. "deltas" has one row per candidate: candidate, its class counts and model, criterion, value, delta_profile (the decrease in the criterion from the converged candidate with one profile fewer, the same group classes and the same structure; positive means this candidate is lower), from_profile naming that candidate, and delta_group_class with from_group_class for one group class fewer. value and both deltas are NA for a candidate that did not converge, and a delta is NA when the smaller neighbour is missing or did not converge. "knees" has one row per line of the grid: direction ("profiles", along the profiles at fixed group classes; "group_classes", along the group classes at fixed profiles; "parameters", every candidate by its number of parameters, one line per structure), line, criterion, from, to, n_points, knee_candidate, distance, knee_without_largest (the knee when the last candidate of the line is left out), stable and note. The knee is the candidate furthest below the straight line from the first to the last candidate, measured perpendicular to it with both axes rescaled to 0-1. This is a simplified rule inspired by Kneedle (Satopaa et al., 2011), without its smoothing or sensitivity thresholds, so a very small positive distance can still name a knee. A line needs three candidates for a knee and four for knee_without_largest and stable; otherwise they are NA and note gives the reason.

"local_dependence"

For a fit with local_dependence: pair, kind ("categorical" or "continuous"), profile, item_1, category_1, item_2, category_2, probability, independent, ratio, covariance and correlation. A categorical pair has one row per profile and category combination, including unobserved combinations subject to the min_probability floor and included in the parameter count: the fitted joint probability, the product of the two marginal probabilities (independent, the joint probability under independence within the profile) and their ratio; its covariance columns are NA. A continuous pair has one row per profile, with the pair's covariance and the correlation it implies; its category and probability columns are NA. A fit without pairs raises latents_no_local_dependence, and what = "all" leaves the table out.

"direct_effects"

For a fit with direct_effects, one row per effect: indicator, covariate, estimate (the change in the indicator's mean per unit of the covariate, the same in every profile), standard_error, statistic, p_value, conf_low and conf_high (Wald, from parameter_inference()). A fit without direct effects raises latents_no_direct_effects, and what = "all" leaves the table out.

"lmr"

The Vuong-Lo-Mendell-Rubin (VLMR) and adjusted Lo-Mendell-Rubin (aLMR) tests of an enumeration grid (Vuong 1989; Lo, Mendell and Rubin 2001; Vermunt 2024), one row per pair of converged candidates that differ by one profile (direction = "profiles") or one group class ("group_classes") at the same structure: direction, null_candidate, alternative_candidate, n_profiles, n_group_classes and model of the alternative, n_units (the independent units scored: groups, or observations without groups), parameters_added, lr (twice the log-likelihood difference), vlmr_p, adjusted_lr (lr / (1 + 1 / (parameters_added * log(n_units)))), almr_p, reference_mean and reference_sd of the weighted chi-square reference distribution, whose weights are the eigenvalues of Vuong's matrix of the two models' scores and Hessians, and note. The p-values are computed by Imhof's method to about 1e-9. A pair whose information matrix is singular, or whose candidate is on a boundary, keeps its row with NA statistics and the reason in note; warnings raised while scoring a candidate are recorded there too. Every candidate's information is computed, so the table is built only when asked for, and what = "all" leaves it out. A grid with no such pair raises latents_no_lmr.

"tree"

The flows of plot_tree(), on every grid, taking its arguments n_group_classes, n_profiles (n_classes on a regression grid), model, candidates, from, to and level (default "individuals"). One row per pair of classes in consecutive rows of each tree: tree (the tree's name, as in the plot list), level, from_candidate, from_class, from_share, to_candidate, to_class, to_share, mass (the share of all units the two classes share, the sum over units of the product of their posterior probabilities, weighted by sampling weights at the individual level), share_of_from and share_of_to (mass as a part of each class). Every pair is listed, including those that share no mass. Units are the rows and groups the fit counts (see drop_empty), weighted by their sampling weights at both levels. A grid with no tree raises latents_no_tree, a fit with a noise component latents_unsupported_noise, and what = "all" leaves the table out. The summary of a grid carries the default table only, without these arguments.

"comparison", "classification"

A compare_models() result. "comparison" is its table, one row per model. "classification", offered when every model is a profile, class, membership-covariate or transition model, has one row per model, level and class: model, then the columns of a fit's "classification" table and that level's relative_entropy; single-class levels are left out. The models themselves are returned by get_candidate().

"test", "replicates"

A bootstrap comparison. "test" is the one-row result; "replicates" has one row per simulated dataset.

"profiles", "responses", "profile_probabilities", "covariances"

A starting-value set: its Gaussian means and variances, response probabilities, profile probabilities and, one row per profile and ordered pair of continuous indicators, its covariances (profile, indicator, indicator_2, covariance).

"entropy", "classification", "average_posteriors", "residuals", "replication"

A diagnostics() object: the tables of the same names described above.

Tables of the other model families

Each family's first table is its default what; "all" returns a named list of every table (without "recovery", which needs data and truth). Tables with intervals take level, and vcov_type ("observed", "robust" or "opg"; NULL reuses the type stored with a regression fit). These objects also have coef(), vcov(type = ), confint(parm = , level = ), logLik() and nobs() methods. confint() of a mixture regression or growth mixture uses the covariance stored with the fit and refuses any other argument with latents_bad_argument (an interval on another covariance is get_results(x, "coefficients", vcov_type = )); vcov() warns latents_unused_argument for an argument it does not take, such as vcov_type = in place of type =.

Mixture regressions (mixture_regression())

"coefficients" (one row per class and term, with Wald statistics, p_adjusted by Benjamini-Hochberg over non-intercepts and exp_estimate for the binomial, Poisson and ordinal families; ordinal thresholds lead each class as terms "threshold:<lower>|<upper>"), "classes", "membership" (multinomial logits and odds ratios), "group_classes" (rows for two-level fits only), "fit" (bic penalised by the number of independent units, bic_rows by the number of rows, as flexmix reports it), "assignments", "groups", "fitted", "starts" (stage "screened" or "completed"), "classification" and "recovery" (by = "class" or "group_class").

Growth mixtures (mixture_regression(random = ))

"coefficients", "classes" (each class's share with its interval, expected_persons, assigned_persons, average_posterior and residual_sd), "membership", "fit", "assignments" (one row per person: class, probability and one posterior_* column per class), "starts" and "recovery", as for a mixture regression, plus "random" (random-effect variances, standard deviations and correlations, with intervals on the log and Fisher-z scales), "random_effects" (one row per person), "trajectories" (each class's mean trajectory with a band) and "individual" (each person's predicted curve); the last two take time. They have no "groups", "fitted" or "classification" table. A multilevel growth mixture adds "group_classes" and "clusters", and its "fit" uses the number of clusters in bic (persons in bic_persons).

Additive fits (multilpa(family = "additive"))

"parameters" (class means, between- and within-group variances and class weights; variance intervals on the log scale, weights on the logit scale; adjust sets the p-value adjustment, "none" by default), "group_classes", "groups", "intercepts" and "conditional_intercepts" (each group's posterior intercept, overall or given each class), "assignments", "classification", "fit", "recovery" and "starts". effective_groups in "group_classes" is w^2 (1 - w) / Var(w), the number of perfectly classified groups that would estimate the class weight as precisely; below 50 the class's intervals carry a latents_weak_class warning.

Cross-level fits (multilpa(family = "full_cross_level") or "restricted_cross_level")

"profiles" (individual profiles, then the group classes' means of group means), "group_classes", "composition" (profile shares within each class: model-implied for the full family, a posterior-weighted description for the restricted one), "groups", "assignments", "fit" and "starts". The likelihood is a working likelihood, comparable only between cross-level fits of the same data.

General transition fits (lta() with transitions = "occasion", transition or initial covariates, measurement = "occasion", order = 2, mover_stayer = TRUE, weights, or ordinal/count indicators)

"transitions" (model-implied, averaged over the observed groups, with their sampling weights in a weighted fit; "initial" and "second_order_transitions" likewise), "transition_coefficients" (log odds of each move against staying, with odds ratios), "second_order_transitions" and "second_order_coefficients" (order = 2), "initial" and "initial_coefficients", "profiles", "responses" (categorical indicators: occasion, profile, indicator, category, probability), "ordinal" and "count_means" (ordinal and count indicators), "group_classes", "assignments", "fit" and "starts".

Pooled imputations (pool_imputations())

"estimates" (the pooled table), "imputations" (each imputation's aligned estimates) and "fits" (one row per imputation).

Transition and group-class family grids (enumerate_classes(time = ), enumerate_classes(family = ))

"candidates" (one row per candidate, its name first, with its likelihood, criteria, entropy and diagnostics) or "best", the row with the lowest criterion ("bic" by groups, the default, "aic" or "bic_individual"). "best" reports the lowest value of a criterion; it does not select a model. With one group class every family is the same model, so those rows share a likelihood. Candidates are extracted by name with get_candidate(); transition grids can also be passed to compare_models().

What "all" returns

A named list of tables included by default for the object, in catalogue order. Some results require an explicit request, including the "lmr" table for an enumeration object. Each included table is built with its default arguments; supplying any further argument raises latents_bad_argument. A table this object cannot produce (for example a sequence table for a fit made without time, or bivariate residuals for a family without discrete group classes) is omitted, so the names of the list show what was available. Only the conditions that mean the table does not exist for this object are skipped; any other error is raised.

Table arguments

These are passed through ...; each table takes only those listed for it under Tables.

data

A data frame with one row per observation of the fit, in the order it was fitted in. NULL uses the columns the fit carries. The standard errors of "profiles" and "responses" come from parameter_inference() on these data. Without data, a fit that cannot supply them (bound-active, unconverged, singular information, a noise component) gives NA with a latents_no_standard_errors message; with data, the underlying condition is raised.

scale

For "profiles": "raw" (default) reports estimates in input units; "standardized" divides each indicator's deviation from its grand mean by that indicator's observed standard deviation, as plot(x, scale = "standardized") draws. The standard errors are divided by the same constant.

format

For the posterior tables and "sequences", "long" (default) gives one row per unit and class and "wide" one row per unit with one column per class. For "information_criteria", "wide" (default) gives one row and "long" one row per criterion and sample-size convention.

level

The classification level to report: "individuals", "groups" or "both". NULL (default) gives "both" for a fit with discrete group classes and "individuals" otherwise, as in diagnostics().

truth

For "assignments", one or more column names of data holding known labels to compare the assignments with. See Recovery.

by

For "residuals", "profile" (default) assesses each profile separately and "overall" pools them.

adjust

For "residuals", the multiplicity correction applied across the indicator pairs: "none" (default) or one of the stats::p.adjust() methods.

definitions

For "information_criteria" in long format, TRUE adds each criterion's formula and reference. Default FALSE.

estimated, stable

For "transitions", TRUE or FALSE restricts the table to the rows estimated (or not) from observed occupancy, or to the diagonal (or off-diagonal) cells. NULL (default) keeps every row.

Recovery

what = "assignments" with truth returns a cross-tabulation of the model's labels against known ones instead of the per-observation table: one row per class and truth value, with columns assignment (the model label compared against), class, truth (the column name), value, n and proportion (the share of units with that truth value assigned to that class). Several truth columns are stacked. Excluded observations or groups appear under class = NA, so the table distinguishes unclassified units from assignments to an estimated class.

A truth column that is constant within every group is compared against group_class; one that varies within any group is compared against profile. The assignment column records which comparison was made. Group-level recovery counts each group once. Unused factor levels are omitted. For a fit without discrete group classes every column is compared against profile.

Class labels are arbitrary, so a truth value assigned mostly to a class with a different label indicates relabelling, not misclassification.

Information criteria

Let q be the number of free parameters, n the chosen sample size, and EN the entropy of the complete-data classification (defined below). The criteria are deviance = -2L, aic = -2L + 2q, bic = -2L + q log(n), sabic = -2L + q log((n + 2) / 24), caic = -2L + q (log(n) + 1), awe = -2(L - EN) + 2q (1.5 + log(n)), icl = -2L + q log(n) + 2 EN, kic = -2L + 3(q + 1), and clc = -2L + 2 EN. clc, like icl and awe, uses the entropy sum; tidyLPA reports a CLC based on relative entropy, and the two values are not comparable. The kic form is Cavanaugh's (1999) criterion as tidyLPA computes it (Rosenberg et al. 2018), with q the number of free parameters; Cavanaugh's general form -2L + 3q is 3 smaller for every model, so differences between models and the model with the smallest value are the same under both.

EN is the soft entropy of the complete-data classification, the entropy term of the classification log likelihood log L_c = log L - EN of ICL (Biernacki, Celeux and Govaert 2000), AWE (Banfield and Raftery 1993) and CLC (Biernacki and Govaert 1997). The latent classification of a two-level model is the group class of every group and the profile of every row, so EN = sum_j H(C_j | y_j) + sum_j sum_h P(C_j = h | y_j) sum_i H(X_ij | C_j = h, y_ij): the group-class entropy plus each row's profile entropy within its group class. With one group class, and in every single-level model, it is the entropy of the profile posteriors. It is the soft form, the posterior expectation of -log P(classes | y) (McLachlan and Peel 2000, section 6.10.3), not the entropy of the modal (hard) assignment that Biernacki, Celeux and Govaert (2000) also discuss. A fit with several group classes saved by latents 0.97.1 or earlier lacks the rows' within-class entropies, and its awe, icl and clc are NA; refit it to obtain them.

Every criterion that depends on a sample size is reported under both multilevel conventions: "groups" with n the number of groups and "individuals" with n the number of rows. EN is the same under both, so the conventions differ only in n, and in a single-level model they coincide. Use one convention consistently across compared candidates. deviance, aic and kic carry convention = NA_character_; clc, which uses no sample size, is the same in both rows. A transition model (lta()) keeps one entropy per level instead: its profiles form a Markov chain within a person, whose path entropy is not the sum of the occasions' entropies. Its "groups" criteria use group-class entropy, whereas its "individuals" criteria use occasion-level profile entropy. These definitions are reported by get_results(x, "information_criteria", format = "long", definitions = TRUE). Individual sample sizes exclude rows with no observed indicators, and group sample sizes exclude groups in which every row has none (n_informative_groups); the entropy and the classification statistics exclude the same rows and groups, as in Mplus. Units of sampling weight zero are in no sample size and no entropy, under either drop_empty. For a fit with sampling weights, L is the pseudo log likelihood and EN the sampling-weighted entropy, each unit's terms multiplied by its weight, so that integer weights give the entropy of the data with each unit repeated that many times. The "entropy" table, relative_entropy, the average posteriors, the odds of correct classification, the classification errors and the BCH weights are weighted the same way; modal counts stay counts.

Classification quality

The odds of correct classification for class k is (p / (1 - p)) / (r / (1 - r)), where p is the average posterior in the assigned class and r is the model-estimated class proportion. Values near one indicate classification no better than the class proportions alone. A value of five is a conventional descriptive benchmark, rather than a formal test of class separation. It is NA_real_ when average_posterior is missing or zero, or when estimated_proportion is zero or one. A perfect average_posterior of one gives Inf at an interior estimated proportion; a single-class solution always reports NA_real_. average_posterior is NA_real_ for a class with no modal members. n_modal and estimated_n use modal assignments and posterior probabilities, respectively, and need not coincide.

relative_entropy is 1 - EN_level / (n log K) (Ramaswamy et al. 1993), between zero and one, higher meaning sharper classification, with EN_level the level's own entropy sum, reported as entropy_sum, lower meaning sharper. With one group class the individual level's entropy_sum is the EN of the information criteria; with several, that EN adds the group-class entropy to the profile entropy within each group class (see Information criteria). relative_entropy is NA_real_ for a level with a single class.

A fit with individual profiles but no discrete group classes reports individuals only for level = "both" and raises latents_no_group_classes for level = "groups".

Bivariate residuals

"residuals" checks, pair by pair, the assumption that indicators are independent within a profile, weighting each observation by its posterior (times its sampling weight). Every pair of indicators has a row (per profile under by = "profile", once under by = "overall"). data must be in the order the model was fitted in; the alignment is checked. Large residuals suggest associations that the measurement model does not adequately represent. Calculations for each kind are described below:

  • "gaussian", two Gaussian indicators: observed is the posterior-weighted correlation of the residuals from the profile's means (pooled over the profiles under "overall"), expected the correlation the fitted covariance implies (zero for a diagonal one). statistic is the difference of their Fisher z transforms times sqrt(effective_n - 3), referred to the standard normal (Fisher, 1921), with a two-sided p-value; df is NA. This is an approximate reference distribution for a posterior-weighted diagnostic.

  • "categorical", two categorical or ordinal indicators (an ordinal indicator's categories are its levels): statistic is the Pearson X^2 of the posterior-weighted two-way table against the table the model implies, which is Latent GOLD's bivariate residual times its df, and p_value refers it to chi-square with df = (R - 1)(C - 1). observed and expected are the two tables' Cramer's V (Cramer, 1946), zero for the model's table within a profile. The chi-square reference ignores that the model's table is estimated from the same data and can therefore be conservative (Oberski, van Kollenburg & Vermunt, 2013). Interpret p_value together with residual and statistic; a non-significant result does not establish conditional independence.

  • "mixed" (a Gaussian and a categorical or ordinal indicator) and "count" (any pair with a count indicator): observed is the posterior-weighted correlation of the two indicators' values within the profile, centred on the profile's weighted means (pooled over the profiles under "overall"); a categorical or ordinal indicator enters as its category number in category order, which for a nominal indicator with more than two categories depends on that order. expected is zero, the correlation of independent indicators, and statistic, df and p_value are NA: no reference distribution is computed for these pairs.

A half-observed row of a joined local_dependence pair enters that pair's tables only where both items are observed. p_adjusted applies the correction named by adjust across the pairs that have a p-value. A fit with sampling weights uses them in the descriptive associations and effective_n; design-based inference is not implemented, so statistic, df, p_value and p_adjusted are NA for weighted fits.

See also

as.data.frame(), which returns the primary table alone, summary(), which prints every table, and diagnostics() for the classification tables with a diagnostic summary.

Examples

fit <- multilpa(
  course_engagement,
  vars = c("browse", "lectures", "forum_read", "forum_post", "attendance"),
  id = "student", n_profiles = 2, n_group_classes = 2, n_starts = 4,
  seed = 1
)
get_results(fit)
#>    profile  indicator       mean  variance standard_deviation

#> 2        1   lectures  0.4274031 0.8446923          0.9190714

#> 9        2 forum_post -0.7526883 0.4211624          0.6489703
#> 10       2 attendance -0.9206599 0.3736293          0.6112523

         truth = c("engagement", "student_type"))
